name: Medial plica syndrome of the knee

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Plicae are embryological remnants of synovial folds, and the medial patellar plica is the one that most often becomes symptomatic
Patients report anteromedial knee pain with clicking or snapping and a sense of catching or pseudo-locking, worse with flexion activities such as stairs or after prolonged sitting
A tender palpable band can often be felt along the medial border of the patella, sometimes rolling under the examining fingers
The plica becomes symptomatic when it thickens, loses elasticity and becomes fibrotic or inflamed through overuse or trauma, impinging on the medial femoral condyle
A chronically inflamed plica can abrade the cartilage of the medial condyle or patella
The diagnosis is largely clinical and one of exclusion, with MRI or dynamic ultrasound able to show a thickened plica
Arthroscopy is the definitive means of confirming a truly pathological plica
Generic management includes activity modification, physiotherapy targeting the quadriceps and stretching, corticosteroid injection and arthroscopic resection for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: A synovial plica is a remnant of the embryonic septa that once divided the knee into compartments, and the medial patellar plica is the fold that most commonly becomes symptomatic. Repetitive overuse or direct trauma causes the plica to thicken, lose its elasticity and become fibrotic and inflamed, so that it impinges against the medial femoral condyle during flexion and extension. This produces pain, snapping and sometimes chondral damage. Asymptomatic plicae are common incidental findings and do not require treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Chondromalacia patellae or a chondral lesion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination for a tender palpable medial band and reproduction of the snap
MRI to show a thickened plica and any associated chondral change
Dynamic ultrasound to visualise the plica during movement
Plain radiographs to exclude other pathology
Diagnostic arthroscopy as the definitive investigation
redFlags: True locking or an effusion suggesting a meniscal tear or loose body
Features suggesting an inflammatory or septic arthritis
reference.prognosis: Many patients settle with conservative treatment, and arthroscopic excision of a genuinely symptomatic plica gives good results.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosis, since asymptomatic plicae are common incidental findings
Missing a meniscal or chondral lesion, as the diagnosis is one of exclusion
Resecting an incidental plica that is not the source of symptoms
management: Begin with conservative care, including activity modification and structured physiotherapy targeting quadriceps and vastus medialis strengthening with hamstring and iliotibial band stretching
Use simple analgesics or NSAIDs to settle the inflamed, fibrotic plica
Consider an intra-articular or local corticosteroid injection for symptoms that persist despite rehabilitation
Address contributing biomechanical factors such as patellar maltracking and training load
Proceed to arthroscopic resection of the symptomatic plica when adequate conservative treatment fails, treating any associated chondral damage at the same time
Refer to orthopaedics for dynamic imaging or arthroscopy where the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are refractory
